newsitem.title: USA: Mideast leaders say little at end of summit.
newsitem.headline: Mideast leaders say little at end of summit.

text.p: The chasm between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was reflected by the scene of them sitting sullenly, side-by-side, staring straight ahead, not talking.
That was the lingering image left from a news conference President Clinton held in the White House East Room to wrap up a high-stakes Middle East summit Wednesday.

A year ago in that same East Room, a beaming Arafat triumphantly signed a new peace accord with then-Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin. There was laughter at the number of jet-lagged participants who fell asleep in the warm confines of the historic room. Rabin was assassinated weeks later.

This time, the two key participants, Arafat and Netanyahu, joined by Jordan's King Hussein, looked as if they were suffering heartburn from their lunch of lamb chops as Clinton announced the summit had produced nothing but a commitment to more talks beginning Sunday.
Arafat, wearing his customary headdress and olive uniform, and Netanyahu, in a dark business suit, looked exhausted and eager to be somewhere else, hands in their lap, looking straight ahead.
When reporters pointed out to Clinton the bizarre sight of three world leaders not participating in a news conference about their region, the president initially put up a defence.
He said they were "certainly free to speak" but that it was his understanding that they wanted him to do it.

"Let's don't kid around -- what we're trying to do is to avoid saying anything that will make our progress more difficult. We want to enhance the chances that we'll actually get something done," Clinton said.
But pressed on the topic again, Clinton finally invited the other leaders to make remarks. Each one in kind waved off the offer, prompting a biblical reference from the president.
"I didn't part the waters, but I have silenced the voices," he said with a laugh.

When it was over, all four men stood together, and photographers shouted for them to shake hands. They waved instead, turned around and walked out of the room on a long red carpet, Arafat moving away from Netanyahu to stroll alongside King Hussein.
Netanyahu later appeared at a news conference at the Mayflower Hotel, while Arafat did not show up for a scheduled appearance at the National Press Club.

When they were leaving the White House to go their separate ways, photographers were called in to record Clinton saying goodbye. Both smiled for the cameras and shook hands, Netanyahu taking Arafat's hand in both of his and pumping it enthusiastically.
For the Israeli leader at least, two days of talks in Washington had not been in vain.
"This was the first step to break down certain barriers that were there, lack of confidence in one another," Netanyahu said at his press conference.
